To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

drilling speed, feed rate (i.e., chip load) and drill diameter have the most significant thermal impacts on bone during drilling, while drill geometry and bone thermal properties have relatively little effect.
the temperature rise and therefore thermal damage during drilling in bone can be reduced by increasing the drill diameter, decreasing the feed rate and increasing the drill rotational speed.

(1) the temperature rise in bone during drilling can be accurately predicted by modeling the heat generation due to machining and heat transfer using finite element analysis; (2) drill speed, feedrate and drill diameter have the greatest effect on temperature rise and thus thermal damage; (3) thermal damage can be predicted by modeling the bone material properties as a function of temperature; and (4) the temperature rise can be reduced by using coolant
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the prediction of the temperature distribution during bone drilling, the prediction of thermal damage, and the development of an optimal drill design.
the development of an improved understanding of the drilling process and how this process affects the bone.
the development of an analytical model that will allow the prediction of temperature rise and thermal damage during drilling of bone.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
drilling in bone at a low speed, high feed rate and with a large drill diameter would result in the lowest thermal damage.
the drill speed, feed, and drill diameter were the most significant parameters that affect thermal injury.

the drill rotational speed and feed rate have the greatest influence on the temperature distribution during bone drilling and that the drill point angle, helix angle and bone thermal property changes had a negligible effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the temperature rise in the bone is directly related to the heat generation during drilling and the thermal conductivity and specific heat of the bone material.
the thermal effects of drilling are not as severe as previously reported and that the thermal injury to bone is primarily a function of the drilling parameters and not of the drill geometry.
drilling in bone is a complex problem that requires a detailed knowledge of bone properties, drilling parameters and drill design.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the thermal impact of the drilling process is a function of the drill speed, feedrate and drill diameter and that it can be reduced by slowing the drill speed, decreasing the feedrate, and increasing the drill diameter.
the thermal damage in the bone is a function of the amount of heat generated and the time over which it is generated, which in turn is dependent on the drill speed, feedrate and drill diameter.
the drill geometry and speed are the main variables that should be controlled to minimize thermal damage in bone during a bone drilling operation.
